title: L-M-D
hook: lamad, limmud, talmid, Talmud: learning and teaching share a root

segments.voice: Yesterday, A-H-V. Your line was ahavah, love: for Rachel, for God, for the neighbor and the stranger. Did you say it out loud to someone? Day one thousand three hundred seventy.

In a beit midrash, a house of study, the room is loud. Two people sit across from each other over one open page. One reads a line aloud. The other says, no, that can't be what it means, and points at the next line. They push back and forth, sometimes for a long while on a few sentences. Who's the teacher here? Watch long enough and it's hard to say. Each one is learning, and each one is teaching, often in the same breath. Hebrew has a root that refuses to keep those two apart, and it's today's word.
screen: `A LOUD ROOM, ONE OPEN PAGE.` → `TWO PEOPLE PUSHING BACK.` → `WHO'S THE TEACHER?`

segments.voice: L-M-D. Lamed, mem, dalet. You met these letters when the roots began, as the example: talmid, melamed, Talmud. Today, what the root does. First, one verse, both ways. At Horeb, God tells Moses to gather the people so "that they may learn to fear me all the days that they shall live upon the earth, and that they may teach their children." Learn, and teach: the same three letters, a few words apart. Second, teach. Later Moses says: "And ye shall teach them your children." The Hebrew is the same root, in a form that means making someone else learn. Learning and teaching aren't two words. They're one root, facing two ways. Third, the book. The collection of rabbinic study, argument and story is called the Talmud, from these same letters. Its name is study. Fourth, who learns from whom. The Talmud, in tractate Taanit, records Rabbi Chanina saying that he learned much from his teachers, more from his friends, and from his students most of all. And the Mishnah, in Pirkei Avot, asks: who is wise? The one who learns from every person. So in this root the teacher is always also a student, and the arrow can point either way across the table. Even the prophet Isaiah uses it in his picture of peace: "neither shall they learn war any more." What people learn, they can also unlearn.
screen: `LEARN THEM, AND KEEP, AND DO THEM.` · `TEACH THEM YOUR CHILDREN.` · `THE TALMUD: A BOOK NAMED STUDY.` · `MOST OF ALL FROM MY STUDENTS.` · then, large: `LEARNING AND TEACHING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: get ready to teach what you've learned. Settle, and breathe. Look back over these roots: shalom, wholeness; bracha, blessing that bends; emet, truth with its first letter; shema, hearing that heeds; teshuvah, turning. Pick the one that stuck. Now shape it into a single sentence you could say to someone over dinner, plainly, with no notes. Say it to yourself once. Then breathe, and let it settle. If you pray, you can bring that sentence into your prayer as something learned. The bell holds the time.
L-M-D. Lamed, mem, dalet: to learn and to teach. The letters of talmid, student, and of the Talmud. Today's word.
Your line: learning and teaching. Today, teach your one sentence to someone, and then ask them what they'd add. Day one thousand three hundred seventy.

howItsDone: Jews study Torah and Talmud in houses of study, synagogues and homes, often in pairs called chavruta, reading aloud and arguing over each line together.
